title: Managing a smallholding in a heatwave
subtitle: Livestock and poultry struggle above 25°C in ways that damage health and production within hours. Most heat stress is preventable with shade, water, and timing adjustments.
excerpt: A heatwave in the UK now means several days above 28°C with warm nights giving no recovery window. Sheep in full fleece, pigs with no sweat glands, and poultry in closed houses are all at serious risk. Here is what to check first and how to prioritise across a mixed holding when conditions are extreme.

glossaryTerms.definition: A condition in livestock where the body cannot dissipate heat fast enough to maintain core temperature. Signs include rapid shallow breathing (panting), reduced feed intake, bunching in shade, excessive salivation, and in severe cases, collapse. Ruminants begin to show heat stress above 25°C when humidity is also high.

A combined measure of temperature and relative humidity used to assess livestock heat stress risk. At THI above 72, most cattle show mild stress; above 80, severe stress is likely. Sheep and pigs are less often assessed by THI but the principle is the same — high humidity at any temperature amplifies heat load because evaporation from the airways is reduced.

Priority order on a mixed holding

Pigs first: pigs cannot sweat and are very susceptible to hyperthermia. They must have wallowing space (a shallow tray of water or a sprinkler system), shade, and cool water throughout the day. Check for panting with an open mouth, this indicates the pig is struggling. If the air temperature inside the pig housing exceeds 30°C, open every ventilation panel and add a portable fan.

Sheep in fleece: sheep shorn in May or June are far lower risk than unsheared animals or sheep sheared late. Unsheared sheep must have access to deep shade throughout the hottest hours (11:00-17:00). Move them into shaded housing if necessary.

Poultry: chickens pant to cool themselves and spread their wings away from their body. At 32°C+ in a closed henhouse, mortality rises fast. Open house doors and mesh panels. Add frozen water bottles to the drinker trays. Reduce feed during the day and offer it in the evening instead, digestion generates heat.

Rabbits: most susceptible above 29°C. Indoor rabbits need frozen water bottles placed against the hutch wall. Outdoor rabbits in direct sun need immediate shade, move hutches or erect a temporary cover.

Water consumption increases 50-100% during heat stress. Check troughs at least three times daily. Top up mid-morning before the peak heat, and again mid-afternoon. Pigs will foul water quickly when hot, refresh pig drinkers more frequently than usual. In extreme heat, add a second drinker if you have one.
A pig lying on its side and not responding to approach, this is an emergency. Move it to shade, wet down with cool (not icy) water, and contact a vet.
Sheep or goats that stagger, lie with neck extended, or breathe very fast need immediate shade. Offer water and check for recovery within 10 minutes.
Any animal not responding to its normal feeding cue during a heatwave requires a hands-on welfare check.
